items.name: ZK rollups
items.does: Let Ethereum check thousands of transactions by verifying one small proof — fees in cents, withdrawals in hours instead of a week.

items.name: Proof of personhood
items.does: Prove to an app that you are a unique human — without revealing which human.

items.name: Private payments
items.does: Send money where sender, receiver and amount stay hidden, yet the network still proves the payment is valid.

items.name: Proof of reserves
items.does: Let an exchange prove it holds every customer's deposit — without publishing any customer's balance.

items.name: zkEmail
items.does: Prove an email says something — a payment confirmation, a ticket, a password reset — without showing the email or your inbox.

items.name: zkTLS / web proofs
items.does: Prove a fact from any website you log into (bank balance above X, your driver rating) without sharing your password or a screenshot.

items.name: zkLogin
items.does: Sign in to a blockchain app with your Google or Apple account — without that identity being linked to you on-chain.

items.name: Private voting
items.does: Vote in an election anyone can audit, where nobody — not even the organiser — can see your ballot.

items.name: Compliance proofs
items.does: Prove your funds do not come from a flagged source — without revealing your transaction history. Returns in the privacy chapter.

zkpCave.heading: Onde está o Wally? — ZK de forma visual

steps.title: A afirmação
steps.text: Digo que encontrei o Wally nesta página enorme e cheia de gente. Não acreditas em mim — e recuso-me a simplesmente apontar, porque isso entrega a minha resposta.

steps.title: A prova
steps.text: Cubro toda a página com uma folha opaca grande que tem um pequeno furo do tamanho do Wally, alinhado exatamente sobre ele. Vês o Wally através do furo.

steps.title: Ficas convencido
steps.text: O Wally está claramente na página — provado. Mas a folha escondeu o resto, por isso continuas sem fazer ideia de ONDE ele está realmente na página.

zkpCave.punchlineA: acabas totalmente convencido de que o Wally lá está, mas não ficas a saber
zkpCave.punchlineB: sobre a localização dele. Esse intervalo é o "zero-knowledge".
zkpCave.classicBody: "a gruta mágica": a Alice sai repetidamente do lado que um verificador grita, provando que conhece a palavra-passe sem nunca a dizer. Repete o suficiente e a sorte fica excluída.

kycSteps.label: O banco emite uma credencial

kycSteps.label: Geras uma prova
kycSteps.desc: Na tua carteira, constróis uma prova STARK: "credencial assinada pelo Banco · idade ≥ 18 · residência = UE · sanções = false". Nenhum dado em bruto é incluído na própria prova.

kycSteps.label: O contrato Cairo verifica
kycSteps.desc: O contrato Cairo da dApp na Starknet verifica a prova e concede acesso. O teu nome e data de nascimento nunca saem da tua carteira — nem sequer o operador da dApp os consegue ler.

dataAvail.subtitle: A proof shows the batch was correct. The data is what lets you leave if the rollup's operator disappears.

svg.userSub: rebuild your balance from L1 data and withdraw, operator or not
svg.caption: Proof without data: you know the books balance but cannot see your own line. The data is what makes the exit possible.

cards.title: What gets posted
cards.desc: Not just a result. A compressed copy of every L2 transaction goes to Ethereum; since 2024 it travels in cheap 'blobs' that Ethereum keeps for about 18 days, long enough for anyone to copy.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.desc: If the rollup's servers go dark, anyone can read the data from Ethereum, rebuild every balance and prove theirs to the L1 bridge to withdraw. Without the data your coins are stuck even though the proof was valid.

cards.title: The cheaper shortcut
cards.desc: Some chains post data to a separate network (Celestia) or a small committee instead. Fees fall, but you now also trust that group to keep the data. Such chains are called validiums or optimiums, and L2BEAT lists them apart from rollups.

privacyApproaches.heading: Quatro formas de obter privacidade on-chain
privacyApproaches.subtitle: Cada uma faz um compromisso diferente entre força, flexibilidade e a forma como os reguladores a tratam.

items.name: Zcash
items.mech: As transações shielded opcionais usam zk-SNARKs para provar a posse e a conservação de valor sem revelar remetente, destinatário ou montante.
items.trade: A privacidade é opt-in, por isso a maior parte do volume mantém-se transparente — enfraquecendo o conjunto de anonimato.

items.name: Monero
items.mech: Privacidade obrigatória: as ring signatures ocultam o remetente, os stealth addresses ocultam o destinatário, o RingCT oculta o montante.
items.trade: Sem opção de transparência — auditar é difícil, por isso muitas exchanges removeram-no da listagem.

items.name: Aztec · Aleo
items.mech: Smart contracts com estado e inputs privados — constrói qualquer dApp confidencial, não apenas pagamentos privados.
items.trade: Muito mais flexível, mas com ferramentas mais recentes (Noir, Leo) e a privacidade vive ao nível do contrato.

items.name: Mixers
items.mech: Juntam muitos depósitos, levantam para endereços novos — quebrando a ligação on-chain entre remetente e destinatário.
items.trade: Credivelmente neutros e imutáveis — que é exatamente por que se tornaram alvo de sanções.

privacyRegulation.cypherpunk: The Cypherpunks (Course 01) said privacy is a precondition for freedom; regulators say untraceable money is a precondition for crime. Both are partly right, which is why selective disclosure (next slide) matters.

privacyRegulation.cypherpunkLabel: Back to where this course began
privacyRegulation.truthB: The same tools protected ordinary people from surveillance — and sanctioning code punished users who had done nothing wrong.
privacyRegulation.truthA: Privacy tools really did shield a state-sponsored hacking group's loot. Regulators had a genuine problem.
privacyRegulation.truthsLabel: Two things are true at once

story.d: A non-custodial mixer on Ethereum: deposit, wait, withdraw to a fresh address. Nobody operates it — the code simply runs.
The US Treasury sanctioned the smart-contract addresses themselves — a first. Its reason: ~$7B laundered, including $455M by North Korea's Lazarus Group. Ordinary users were swept in too.
Alexey Pertsev convicted in the Netherlands (64 months, under appeal); Roman Storm awaiting trial in the US. Writing privacy software itself became the legal question.
A US appeals court ruled immutable smart contracts are not "property" that can be sanctioned. OFAC delisted Tornado Cash on 21 March 2025.
Storm convicted on one count (unlicensed money transmission); the jury hung on laundering and sanctions charges. Samourai Wallet's founders received 4–5 years (Nov 2025).

quiz.question: Um utilizador levanta fundos da Arbitrum (um optimistic rollup) de volta para a Ethereum L1. O levantamento padrão demora ~7 dias. Porquê?
options: O tempo de bloco da L1 é mais lento do que o da L2, por isso a L1 tem de recuperar o atraso antes de processar o levantamento.

Os optimistic rollups assumem as transações válidas por defeito. A "janela de contestação" de 7 dias permite a qualquer pessoa submeter uma fraud proof se o estado da L2 for inválido; até essa janela fechar, os levantamentos não podem ser finalizados com segurança na L1.
A Arbitrum agrupa os levantamentos semanalmente para amortizar os custos de gas entre os utilizadores.
A Ethereum L1 limita deliberadamente a taxa de levantamentos das L2 para evitar congestão induzida pelos rollups.
quiz.explanation: O atraso de 7 dias é estrutural ao modelo de optimistic rollup. O sequencer da L2 publica state roots na L1 com o pressuposto de que são válidos; qualquer pessoa que vigie a chain pode contestar uma root inválida submetendo uma fraud proof durante a janela de contestação. Até essa janela expirar, a L1 não pode confiar o suficiente na state root para libertar levantamentos. Os ZK rollups não têm este atraso — cada lote vem com uma prova de validade que a L1 verifica criptograficamente, por isso os levantamentos podem ser finalizados num bloco L1. Bridges rápidas de terceiros (Across, Hop, Stargate) permitem aos utilizadores saltar a espera pagando antecipadamente um pequeno prémio a fornecedores de liquidez.

quiz2.question: Uma equipa está a lançar uma nova blockchain específica para a sua app. Precisam de controlo total sobre o algoritmo de consenso, o token de gas e a governação de upgrades. Que modelo encaixa melhor — e qual é o compromisso?
options: Parachain da Polkadot via Coretime — soberania dentro do envelope de segurança partilhada da relay chain, sem compromisso.
Cosmos zone via Cosmos SDK — soberania total sobre consenso, gas e upgrades; o compromisso é arrancar com o seu próprio conjunto de validadores sem herdar qualquer segurança externa.
Avalanche L1 — chains soberanas, mas têm de usar o consenso Snowman e pagar taxas de subscrição denominadas em AVAX.
As três dão soberania igual; a decisão é puramente impulsionada pelo custo.
quiz2.explanation: As Cosmos zones são soberanas por design. Cada chain escolhe o seu próprio motor de consenso (o CometBFT é o predefinido, mas vale tudo), o seu próprio token de gas, as suas próprias regras de governação e upgrade. O compromisso é real: a equipa tem de recrutar validadores, desenhar segurança económica e arrancar com um token de valor para os pagar — nenhuma segurança partilhada vem de graça. As parachains da Polkadot partilham o conjunto de validadores da relay chain (ótimo), mas têm de se conformar ao modelo de runtime da relay e ao calendário de Coretime (menos soberania que o Cosmos). As Avalanche L1s (antigas Subnets, renomeadas via ACP-13/77 em 2024) permitem VMs personalizadas e subconjuntos de validadores, mas na prática a maioria corre variantes do Snowman e paga taxas de validador em AVAX. O enquadramento honesto: segurança partilhada versus soberania é um compromisso, não uma lista hierárquica.

takeaways.title: Secção 05 — Conclusões
items: Os ZK rollups usam provas de validade criptográficas — sem janela de contestação, finalidade instantânea, e a base para privacidade verificável
Os optimistic rollups (Arbitrum, Base, Optimism) oferecem compatibilidade EVM total com menor custo computacional — ao preço de um atraso de levantamento de 7 dias
Cada L2 tem uma cultura distinta: Arbitrum para profundidade de DeFi, Base para apps de consumo, Starknet para jogos e computação ZK-nativa
A privacidade em chains públicas exige maquinaria criptográfica adicional — a linha regulatória para "ferramentas de privacidade" ainda está a ser traçada
Faz cinco perguntas antes de escolher uma plataforma: permissão, programabilidade, débito, privacidade e soberania

keyPoints.s5-zkp: Prove it is true without showing why.
keyPoints.s5-zkp-cave: A proof convinces by making cheating impossible, not by showing the secret.
keyPoints.s5-zk-apps: ZK is a product, not a paper: scaling, identity, solvency and compliance proofs are live today.
keyPoints.s5-zk-identity: Verify the claim, not the person: the issuer vouches once and the customer reveals only what each service needs.
keyPoints.s5-l2-why: You cannot max out speed, cost and decentralisation at once; L2s buy speed by borrowing L1 security.
keyPoints.s5-layer2: Optimistic rollups are innocent until proven guilty (7-day exit), ZK rollups are proven before accepted (hours), and neither is private by default.
keyPoints.s5-data-avail: A rollup is only as safe as the data behind it; posting every transaction to Ethereum is what lets users leave without the operator's help.
keyPoints.s5-starknet: Starknet uses ZK for cheap verification, not secrecy.
keyPoints.s5-polkadot: Polkadot rents out security; parachains skip recruiting validators but live by the Relay Chain's rules.
keyPoints.s5-avalanche: Avalanche sells sovereign lanes with shared tooling; a custom L1 is only as secure as its own validators.
keyPoints.s5-privacy: A public ledger is a permanent record; privacy has to be added on purpose.
keyPoints.s5-privacy-approaches: Mixers hide everything or nothing; ZK reveals exactly what a counterparty needs.
keyPoints.s5-privacy-regulation: Untraceable money shields dissidents and launderers alike; selective disclosure is the way out.
keyPoints.s5-privacy-future: Keep the data confidential and still prove you follow the rules.
keyPoints.s5-evaluate: Judge a project by who built it, what the code says and who holds the tokens.
keyPoints.s5-evaluate-2: Locked liquidity, honest docs and organic on-chain usage; ten minutes with free tools beats any influencer thread.
keyPoints.s5-decision: Five questions beat a hundred logos: permission, programmability, throughput, privacy, sovereignty.

starknet.heading: Starknet — a ZK rollup on Ethereum
starknet.subtitle: Thousands of transactions run off-chain; one STARK proof tells Ethereum they were all executed correctly.
starknet.recap: Section 02 · Rollups & L2s — and the ZK chapter above

cards.label: What it is
cards.title: Ethereum's security, Starknet's speed
cards.body: A Layer 2 that batches transactions, proves the batch with a STARK and posts only the proof to Ethereum. If the proof is wrong, Ethereum rejects the batch — no waiting period, no trust in the operator.

cards.label: What it's good at
cards.title: Cheap verification + smart wallets
cards.body: Fees 10–100× below L1 and withdrawals in hours, not a week. Every account is a smart contract by default (account abstraction): social recovery, session keys, fees paid in any token.

cards.label: One real app
cards.title: Ekubo — a DEX from a former Uniswap lead
cards.body: A concentrated-liquidity exchange with the deepest liquidity on Starknet. Fully on-chain games (Realms: Eternum, Loot Survivor) are the other main use.

cards.label: The caveat
cards.title: Public by default, Cairo only
cards.body: ZK here buys cheap verification, not secrecy — transactions are as visible as on Ethereum. Apps must be written in Cairo, so Solidity code cannot be copied over unchanged, and the ecosystem is far smaller than Arbitrum or Base.

polkadot.heading: Polkadot — security for rent
polkadot.subtitle: A Layer 0: one Relay Chain whose validators secure every connected parachain at once.

cards.label: What it is
cards.title: One validator set, many chains
cards.body: Parachains are purpose-built L1s that rent block time (Coretime) on the Relay Chain instead of recruiting their own validators. The Relay Chain's ~300 validators finalise all of them together.

cards.label: What it's good at
cards.title: Day-one security and native cross-chain calls
cards.body: A new chain is as secure as Polkadot the moment it connects. Parachains talk to each other through XCM — a built-in message format — so no bridge contract and no wrapped token inside the ecosystem.

cards.label: One real app
cards.title: Moonbeam — Ethereum apps, Polkadot plumbing
cards.body: An EVM-compatible parachain where Solidity contracts deploy unchanged and can call other parachains over XCM. It is the usual entry point for Ethereum teams testing the ecosystem.

cards.label: The caveat
cards.title: Rules of the club, and a thin crowd
cards.body: Chains must follow Relay Chain rules and pay for coretime in DOT; user and developer traction has lagged Ethereum's L2s; and reaching chains outside Polkadot still needs a bridge (Snowbridge to Ethereum).

avalanche.heading: Avalanche — sovereign lanes, shared tooling
avalanche.subtitle: A Layer 0 whose Primary Network coordinates custom 'Avalanche L1s', each with its own validators and rules.

cards.label: What it is
cards.title: A primary network plus custom L1s
cards.body: Three built-in chains (X, P and the EVM C-Chain, where DeFi lives) plus any number of Avalanche L1s (formerly Subnets): sovereign chains that pick their own validators, gas token and rules, coordinated by the P-Chain.

cards.label: What it's good at
cards.title: Sub-second finality and your own lane
cards.body: Snowman consensus settles in under a second. A game or a bank can launch its own L1 with custom fees and permissioning, reuse Ethereum tooling, and message other L1s natively through Avalanche Warp.

cards.label: One real app
cards.title: JP Morgan on a permissioned L1
cards.body: JP Morgan's Onyx (now Kinexys) and Apollo tested tokenised-portfolio management on Avalanche's institutional 'Evergreen Spruce' network under Singapore's Project Guardian (2023).

cards.label: The caveat
cards.title: Small validator sets, fragmented liquidity
cards.body: A sovereign L1 is only as secure as its own validators, often a handful. Finality is probabilistic (a tiny chance of reversal, unlike BFT's hard guarantee), and most liquidity still sits on the C-Chain.

discussion.eyebrow: In-class discussion · ~10 min · nothing to hand in
discussion.prompt: Pick one: which platform would you choose — and what are you trading away?
discussion.subtitle: Choose a scenario, pick a platform from this course, and name the trade-off. The reasoning is the point.

scenarios.title: A bank tokenises a money-market fund
scenarios.desc: A European bank wants to issue a tokenised fund to institutional clients, with regulators watching every step.

scenarios.title: A mobile game with millions of micro-trades
scenarios.desc: Players trade in-game items thousands of times a minute and expect ownership that outlives the studio.

scenarios.title: Aid payments where banks are unreliable
scenarios.desc: An NGO must pay thousands of recipients in a country with a shaky banking system — without exposing who they are.

questions: Who has to trust whom in your design — and would the people involved accept that?
What does the choice cost you later: lock-in, bridge risk, regulatory exposure, a thin ecosystem?
Would a plain database do the job? If yes, say so — that is also a valid answer.
